meta.title: AstroPIE-53: Towards Understanding Failure Modes of Human Pose Estimation in Space
meta.authorsHtml: Stephanie Käs <sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Marten Flaig<sup>1</sup>, Lukas Woyke<sup>1</sup>, Osmanalp Ömeroğlu<sup>1</sup>, Felix Krückel<sup>1</sup>, Onur Alp Çulha<sup>1</sup>, Bastian Leibe<sup>1</sup>

meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: Reliable monitoring of astronauts is essential for safety, situational awareness, and autonomous assistance in space missions. While modern computer vision enables accurate human detection and pose estimation on Earth, its robustness in space environments remains largely unquantified due to limited data availability. We present AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of 53 annotated astronaut videos collected from publicly available mission footage. To respect copyright restrictions, we release video identifiers, reconstruction scripts, and dense annotations rather than raw videos. The dataset includes bounding boxes, challenge classes, and human-annotated pose failure tags. We benchmark state-of-the-art person detection and pose estimation models under realistic zero-shot deployment conditions and perform the first systematic failure analysis for astronaut monitoring. Our results reveal substantial performance degradation caused by occlusions, unusual body orientations, low contrast, and microgravity motion patterns.

blocks.html: As human presence remains relevant for space exploration, ensuring astronaut safety is crucial for future missions. Autonomous monitoring of astronaut activity enables health assessment, hazard detection, and human–robot collaboration. Several studies have investigated astronaut motion using multisensor systems or marker-based motion capture [1–6], which increases payload and system complexity. Thus, human pose estimation relying solely on onboard cameras without any additional sensors would be beneficial. Modern computer vision methods offer such approaches for markerless human monitoring, being highly accurate in person detection and body pose estimation in terrestrial environments. However, their robustness under real space conditions remains largely unexplored. Space environments introduce severe domain shifts compared to standard vision datasets: unique visual characteristics including microgravity body orientations, bulky spacesuits, occlusions, and extreme image contrast variability. Publicly available astronaut imagery is scarce due to legal and operational constraints.

No prior work systematically provides a quantitative analysis of how modern detection and pose estimation pipelines perform on authentic astronaut mission footage. We address this gap by (1) presenting AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of real astronaut videos with bounding box annotations, structured challenge classes, and pose failure tags.

blocks.html: (2) Using AstroPIE-53, we benchmark modern person detection and pose estimation models on authentic mission footage. (3) We then propose a taxonomy of space-specific visual challenges and quantify their impact on detection and pose estimation failures.

Human Pose Estimation. Vision-based human pose estimation (HPE) reconstructs human skeletons or meshes from images. Modern pipelines typically follow a twostage approach: (1) person localization using object detectors (such as YOLO [13], DETR [11] ), foundation models (like DINO [12], Gemini [14]) which create bounding boxes around the person or body segmentation masks [15]. (2) Using these body selections, pose estimation methods (such as MeTRAbs [7], NLF [9], and ViTPos [16]) reconstruct human models. Other methods - like OpenPose [17] - directly estimate potential body joints and assign them to persons afterwards. Skeletons/meshes can then be used for tasks such as gesture/activity recognition [18].

Astronaut Monitoring Most existing approaches (Table 1) use a single camera (monocular). AstroPose [19] formulates pose estimation without the use of AI as a geometric optimization problem. Later works adopt CNN-based pipelines: SpacesuitPose [20] enhances HRNet [21] with occlusion-aware augmentation and structural losses, µPose [22] demonstrates improvements through synthetic microgravity fine-tuning, and ROpenPose [23] proposes a lightweight OpenPose [17] variant optimized for real-time posture tracking. H3-AstroPoseNet [24] uses multi-camera views, but lacks evaluation on space-like data.

Relevant Datasets. Though many terrestrial HPE datasets exist (e.g. COCO [25], EgoExo4D [26]), existing astronaut HPE datasets are small and limited in diversity and availability (Table 1). SpacesuitPose provides 400 annotated frames from EVA and training footage, while NASA’s Spacesuit Detection Challenge [8] released a small dataset that is no longer publicly accessible. AstroPose combines marker-based recordings with unannotated mission footage. µPose introduces synthetic microgravity avatars in a single ISS-like environment, and OpenPose contributes an indoor capsule dataset focused mainly on posture classification. Spacewalk-18 [27] introduces a long-form video understanding benchmark for space operation scenarios, but does not focus on person detection, pose estimation nor does it provide a failure analysis. In contrast, our dataset AstroPIE-53 includes more than 20k annotated frames with 2D bounding boxes and pose failure cases.

Failure Sources. Prior work mentions challenges such as occlusions, bulky suits, lighting variability, and microgravity motion patterns. However, these factors are rarely quantified, and no study quantitatively analyzes failure sources across the full detection–pose pipeline. We address this gap by presenting a quantitative failure analysis of pose detection and pose estimation models on real astronaut recordings using our AstroPIE-53 dataset.
We introduce AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset designed to analyze failure modes in vision-based astronaut monitoring from real mission footage.
Data Collection: We collected 53 videos from publicly available astronaut recordings published by space agencies.

blocks.html: The footage spans intra-vehicular and extra-vehicular activities, including maintenance tasks, tours, and mission operations. To construct the dataset, we developed a semiautomated three-stage pipeline consisting of Search, Synchronization, and Annotation (see Figure 2). In the Search stage, candidate videos are identified using keyword-based queries and stored as structured metadata (video IDs, titles, timestamps, and URLs). The Sync stage filters and downloads relevant videos while ensuring consistency between the metadata repository and the local dataset. Finally, the Annotate stage processes the synchronized videos to extract frames and generate annotations. To respect copyright restrictions, raw videos are not redistributed. Instead, we release reconstruction scripts, video identifiers, and annotations, enabling researchers to deterministically reconstruct the dataset from publicly available sources.

Annotations: We manually annotated three types of labels using a custom GUI (??): (1) Bounding Boxes: Manual astronaut detection annotations (20.5k frames).(2) Failure Tags: Human-annotated error categories describing failures of outputs. Failure tags are assigned per astronaut track and may be multi-label. (3) Challenge Classes: Environmental tags including occlusion, low illumination, suit presence, person-camera orientation, and camera distance. We structure AstroPIE-53 accordingly (see Table 2).
We analyze failure modes of vision-based astronaut monitoring using a representative detection–pose pipeline, providing a broad coverage of state-of-the-art detection and pose estimation strategies.

Person Detection: We evaluate three complementary object detection paradigms: YOLO26 [10] represents highspeed convolutional detectors commonly used in real-time robotics applications. RF-DETR [11] is a transformer-based detector designed for robust localization under scale variation and clutter. Grounding DINO [12] is a foundation detection model that leverages vision–language alignment and enables open-vocabulary detection via text prompts. These models were selected to cover the dominant detection paradigms currently deployed in real-world perception systems, ranging from conventional CNN detectors to modern transformer and foundation-model approaches.

Pose Estimation: For pose estimation, we evaluate three representative top-down methods: CNN-based Me- TRAbs [7] performs direct regression of 3D human skeletons and is known for robustness to viewpoint variation and compatibility with fisheye cameras [28]. NLF [9] reconstructs parametric human meshes using neural body models, enabling detailed structural predictions. ViTPose [16] is transformer–based using global attention [29] to predict body keypoints.
We evaluate representative state-of-the-art models on AstroPIE-53 and its challenge class subsets (without retraining) to simulate realistic deployment conditions.

We benchmark Grounding DINO [12], RF-DETR [11], and YOLO26 [10] on astronaut detection using AstroPIE-53 challenge subsets. RF-DETR [11] and YOLO26 [10] rely on fixed label sets. Only detections classified as person are considered, as there is no astronaut class. Grounding DINO uses text prompts and is evaluated using both astronaut and person with a text threshold of τtext = 0.25. As an evaluation metric, we use the AP@50 metric, measuring the Average Precision at an Intersection-over-Union (IoU) threshold τIoU = 0.5 and report the results in Table 3. We selected the confidence thresholds (τconf = 0.3) based on our ablation studies (Section 5.2).

Results & Interpretation: As seen in Table 3, detection performance is substantially higher without spacesuits among all three detectors. Frontal views yield the best (DINO: ∼95%, Others: ∼86%), whereas back views significantly reduce performance (All: ≤25%, YOLO: ∼2%), with side and multi-view cases in between. This might be caused by large backpacks carried by astronauts. Environmental conditions follow a similar pattern to viewing angles since outdoor recordings exclusively contain astronauts wearing spacesuits. Image contrast strongly affects performance: high contrast improves AP@50, while low contrast degrades it (All: ≤25%). Large camera distances lead to the strongest performance drop (DINO: ≤23%, Others: ≤1%) and represent the most challenging scenario. Unexpectedly, occluded frames yield higher AP, likely reflecting viewpoint, distance and contrast rather than occlusion itself. The comparison clearly shows that DINO significantly outperforms YOLO26 and RF-DETR on AstroPIE-53, which basically fail to detect anything in outdoor scenarios, at low contrast and far distances.

blocks.html: We compare different τconf and τIoU for Grounding DINO [12], RF-DETR [11], and YOLO26 [11] on astronaut detection using AstroPIE-53.

F1–confidence curves for IoU thresholds of 0.5 and 0.75. Grounding DINO with the astronaut prompt achieves the highest F1 score at both IoU levels, peaking around τconf = 0.3. The person prompt follows a similar trend but with slightly lower performance. YOLO variants exhibit more stable behavior across confidence thresholds, particularly at higher confidence levels, where their F1 scores remain comparatively consistent. In contrast, RF-DETR variants show low precision at τconf ≤0.2 and overall lower F1 scores. Performance decreases when increasing the τIoU from 0.5 to 0.75, but the relative ranking of the models remains largely consistent.

Since ground-truth pose annotations are unavailable for real mission footage, we perform a structured humanannotated failure analysis rather than reporting classical pose accuracy metrics. For each astronaut track, predicted pose sequences from MeTRAbs [7], NLF [9], and ViTPose [16] are labeled with predefined failure categories: misaligned body parts, incorrect scale, wrong global orientation, fully misaligned poses, temporal jitter, and shadowing. We use AstroPIE-53 ground-truth bounding boxes to isolate pose estimation errors from detection errors.

blocks.html: Results. Table 4 reports failure prevalence as a percentage of annotated keyframes. Fully misaligned poses are the dominant failure, affecting 57.2% (ViTPose), 43.3% (MeTRAbs), and 30.9% (NLF) of keyframes, potentially due to microgravity-related unusual body orientations. Vit- Pose exhibits the highest jitter rate (9.8%), while NLF is affected by scale (3.4%) and global orientation errors (3.8%). Leg misalignment is the most common partial-body failure, peaking at 8.5% for MeTRAbs. NLF provides the highest proportion of correct estimates, with 69.8% of frames being correctly annotated, while ViTPose provides the lowest accuracy at 48.3%. No pose estimator dominates across all failure modes.

We introduce AstroPIE-53, the first dataset enabling systematic evaluation of vision-based astronaut monitoring. Our experiments demonstrate significant performance degradation of modern detection and pose estimation pipelines on authentic mission footage. By providing a reproducible dataset curation pipeline, systematic taxonomy of challenges for astronaut detection in space, and quantitative failure analysis, this work aims to draw attention to open research questions in astronaut monitoring.
